what_its_for: Propafenone is used to treat certain types of irregular heartbeats (called arrhythmias). It helps your heart beat in a more normal, steady rhythm. Your doctor may prescribe it for conditions like atrial fibrillation (AFib), atrial flutter, or other fast or irregular heart rhythms.
how_to_take: Take propafenone exactly as your doctor tells you. The regular tablets (Rythmol) are usually taken 2 to 3 times a day. The extended-release capsules (Rythmol SR) are taken twice a day. You can take this medicine with or without food, but try to take it the same way each time. Swallow extended-release capsules whole — do not crush, chew, or open them. Take it at the same times every day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your heart condition and how your body responds to the medicine. Common starting doses for adults are 150 mg three times a day for regular tablets, or 225 mg twice a day for extended-release capsules. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose if needed. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one, as this could cause serious heart problems.
storage: Store propafenone at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking propafenone, as they can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid alcohol, as it may increase dizziness. Do not start, stop, or change any other medicines — including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal supplements — without asking your doctor or pharmacist first, since many medicines can interact with propafenone. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause dizziness or blurred vision.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a new or worsening irregular heartbeat or feel your heart pounding or fluttering; chest pain or tightness; severe dizziness or fainting; shortness of breath; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain; unusual bruising or bleeding; fever, chills, or signs of infection; or swelling in your legs or feet. Also call your doctor if you feel unusually tired, have blurry vision, or notice any new or bothersome symptoms.
when_it_works: Propafenone begins working fairly quickly — often within a few hours of taking the first dose. However, it may take several days to weeks before your heart rhythm is fully controlled and you feel the full benefit of the medicine. Keep taking it even if you feel well. Do not stop taking propafenone without talking to your doctor first, as stopping suddenly can be dangerous.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): You may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness or low blood pressure. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and monitor you more closely. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Propafenone should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed, as the risks to the baby are not fully known. Breastfeeding: This medicine may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking propafenone. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more frequently if you have kidney or liver disease. Children: Propafenone is not commonly prescribed for children and should only be used under close medical supervision.
